hook: Tell a story that goes wrong, in German, and find out which tense slipped.
intro: Narrating is harder than reporting, because the tenses have to hold together across a whole text. Write what you had planned, what happened, what you did and how it ended. Aim for 400 to 900 characters. Two things earn the marks: the spoken past mix, which is Präteritum for war, hatte and the modal verbs and Perfekt for everything that happened, and one Plusquamperfekt in the right place, marking the thing that had already happened before the rest.
tips[0].title: The mix that sounds natural
tips[0].text: Written German narration leans on the Präteritum, but in a personal story the natural mix is Präteritum for sein, haben and the modal verbs and Perfekt for the actions. Mixing them that way is not sloppy; it is what a German speaker does.
tips[0].check.why: sein is told in the Präteritum even when the actions around it are Perfekt.
tips[0].trap: Do not put the actions in the Präteritum too unless you are writing literature: „ich verpasste den Zug“ is correct but reads like a novel.
tips[1].title: The Plusquamperfekt marks what came first
tips[1].text: When one past event happened before another, the earlier one takes hatte or war plus the participle. It is what makes a story read in order even when you tell it out of order.
tips[1].check.why: nachdem puts the earlier event in the Plusquamperfekt: hatten gegessen.
tips[1].visual.marks[0].label: before the story
tips[1].visual.marks[1].label: the story
tips[2].title: A story needs a turn
tips[2].text: Plan, then the turn, then what you did, then the end. The turn is what makes it a story: plötzlich, auf einmal, doch dann. Without it you have written a timetable.
tips[2].check.why: plötzlich marks the moment the plan breaks; the others add or explain.
remember[0]: Präteritum for war, hatte and the modals; Perfekt for the actions.
remember[1]: nachdem plus Plusquamperfekt, then Präteritum or Perfekt in the main clause.
remember[2]: eigentlich sets up the plan, plötzlich breaks it, schließlich ends it.
remember[3]: A story has a turn; a list does not.
exam: Telling a past story in writing is the narrative task the B1 certificate sets, and the one everyone tells at a dinner table.
mistakes[0].why: nachdem needs the earlier event one step further back.
mistakes[1].why: sein is told in the Präteritum.
mistakes[2].why: The departure happened first, so it takes the Plusquamperfekt.
mistakes[3].why: Three bare sentences are a list; connectors make it a story.
